title: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade: A Public Health Crisis 95% of Locals Want Ended
excerpt: With 5 million dogs killed annually and zero regulated slaughterhouses, Vietnam's uncontrolled dog meat trade poses severe rabies and food safety risks. New government roadmap aims for phase-out by 2030—backed by overwhelming public support.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam's dog meat trade kills an estimated 5 million animals annually through completely unregulated supply chains, creating a documented public health crisis. In January 2026, Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment unveiled a roadmap to phase out the trade by 2030, aligned with the country's rabies elimination goals. Critically, 95% of Vietnamese surveyed oppose the trade—meaning this isn't a cultural battle, but a public health emergency with overwhelming local consensus.

Key Findings

Rabies Deaths Spike as Stolen Dogs Enter Unvetted Supply Chains

Vietnam recorded a 160% rise in human rabies fatalities in early 2025, with public health officials directly linking the surge to the dog meat trade's disruption of vaccination efforts. Dogs trafficked for meat—often stolen pets lacking any health certification—arrive at markets without quarantine checks, creating a direct transmission vector. Hanoi's CDC reports approximately 70–100 annual rabies deaths, mostly from dog bites, with disease transmission risk compounded by the practice of force-feeding animals contaminated scraps during transport.

Stolen Pets Now Supply Majority of Trade; Nearly 10,000 Dogs Taken Since 2022

FOUR PAWS documented nearly 10,000 stolen dogs and cats between late 2022 and 2024, with organized gangs operating across provinces using electric stun guns and motorcycles for night-time raids. This shift toward pet theft reflects Vietnam's rising pet ownership (now 20% of households) and explains escalating public anger. Critically, dog theft prosecutions rarely occur unless animals exceed VND 2 million (~$86) in value, allowing criminal networks to operate with near-total impunity. The supply chain remains completely unregistered—no slaughterhouses are licensed, meaning zero food safety oversight or disease surveillance.

Government Roadmap Reflects 95% Public Opposition; Phase-Out by 2030 Targets Rabies Control

Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment presented a structured phase-out roadmap at a January 2026 high-level meeting, framing elimination not as cultural restriction but as public health necessity. The proposal emphasizes coordinated enforcement, improved animal vaccination programs, and behavioral change communication across provinces. Polling data shows 64% of Vietnamese support a dog meat ban, 68% support banning the trade itself, and 95% reject the narrative that consumption is culturally essential. This represents the clearest evidence to date that phasing out the trade aligns with—rather than contradicts—Vietnamese public values.

Food Safety Crisis: E. coli, Salmonella, and Contaminated Meat Dominate Health Warnings

Vietnamese health authorities warn that 88% of surveyed Vietnamese view dog meat as a health risk, with 44% specifically citing disease concerns. Beyond rabies, the unregulated supply chain enables trichinosis (parasitic infection from undercooked meat), cholera, and bacterial contamination. Dogs are transported in cramped, unsanitary conditions without food or water, arriving sick or deceased at markets. Forged documents at checkpoints and complete absence of veterinary inspection mean no traceability, no disease testing, and no accountability. The result: meat deemed unfit for human consumption enters informal food networks, amplifying infection risk across communities.

Also Worth Noting

  • Los Angeles Conditional Sister-City Pact — In April 2025, LA City Council introduced a motion linking sister-city status with Hanoi to a commitment to ban the dog meat trade, signaling international pressure aligning with local Vietnamese public opinion.
  • Parliamentary Handbook on Animal Welfare — Vietnam's National Assembly launched guidance for delegates to strengthen companion animal protection laws, directly addressing loopholes enabling the unregulated trade.
  • Rabies Quarantine Law Enforcement Accelerates — Organizations like Animals Asia are leveraging existing animal health regulations to disrupt illegal transport, with success in documenting supply chains and building cases for prosecution.
  • Hội An Moves Toward Dog-Meat-Free Status — The tourist city is voluntarily transitioning to become Vietnam's first dog-meat-free municipality through business cooperation, demonstrating market viability of phase-out models.
  • Circular No. 01/2026 Tightens Animal Quarantine Standards — Effective January 1, 2026, new regulations on terrestrial animal quarantine provide legal tools to intercept illegally transported dogs destined for slaughter.
  • Major Dog Theft Rings Dismantled — In February 2026, Gia Lai police arrested six traffickers responsible for stealing over 5,200 dogs (52 tons), generating 2.6 billion VND in illegal revenue—illustrating both the scale and growing enforcement response.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030. With 95% of Vietnamese already opposed to the trade, your voice adds to an overwhelming local consensus demanding change.
